analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare payments to hospitals and nursing homes owned by private equity firms or real estate trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2026 with three Democratic sponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has received no vote, hearing, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut off all Medicare payments to hospitals and nursing homes owned or controlled by private equity funds, companies owned by such funds, or real estate investment trusts (REITs). Facilities already owned by those firms would get three years to sell or lose Medicare money. The goal is to stop investment firms from owning hospitals as profit-making assets.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare patients treated at hospitals and nursing homes owned by private equity or REITs, and the communities that rely on those facilities. Private equity ownership of hospitals has been widely studied as a driver of cost-cutting, staffing reductions, and facility closures, so removing Medicare dollars from that ownership model is meant to protect care at facilities patients depend on.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans Medicare payments to any hospital or skilled nursing facility owned or controlled by a private equity fund, a corporation owned by such a fund, or a real estate investment trust.
Existing private equity- or REIT-owned facilities get a three-year grace period before the payment ban applies, giving them time to sell to new owners.

A covered firm that owns a violating facility is jointly and severally liable for any penalty the facility receives, making the parent firm directly accountable rather than letting an individual hospital take the fall.
The bill defines control broadly, reaching ownership of 10% or more of voting securities and management contracts, so firms could not easily evade the ban through shell structures.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds and REITs that own hospitals or nursing homes. They would have three years to divest, or they would lose Medicare revenue — typically the largest single source of income for a hospital — which would force sales, restructuring, or in some cases closure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity firms and hospital REITs

drawbacks.text: The enforcement tool is blunt: any facility still owned by a covered firm after three years loses all Medicare payments, and if no buyer can be found, the facility could close — leaving the community with less access, not more.

REITs frequently own hospital buildings and land as a financing arrangement rather than running the medical operation; a blanket ownership ban could disrupt hospital financing and force restructuring even where patient care is not the problem.
Because Medicare is often a hospital's largest payer, the cutoff could push some owners to cut staffing or defer maintenance while scrambling to divest, rather than improving care in the interim.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The aim — ending private equity ownership of hospitals and nursing homes — responds to real harm: investment-firm ownership has been linked to cost-cutting that affects patients. But the bill's single remedy, cutting off Medicare payments entirely, is severe. A better-designed law might bar acquisitions prospectively and police staffing and pricing at existing facilities; this bill risks closing some facilities that patients need. The three-year divestment window softens but does not remove that risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it now sits in committee.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Murphy introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, joined by Senators Blumenthal and Merkley.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action appears in the record.

The bill would prohibit Medicare payments to hospitals and skilled nursing facilities owned by private equity funds, firms they own or control, or real estate investment trusts, with a three-year exemption for facilities already owned by such firms on the date of enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As things stand, private equity funds and REITs that own hospitals and nursing homes benefit: the Medicare revenue at those facilities continues uninterrupted while the bill sits without action in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and REIT owners of hospitals

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors are Democrats, and the Republican-chaired Senate Finance Committee has not moved the bill since referral.

industries.industry: Private equity firms that own hospitals and nursing homes
industries.note: These firms would lose Medicare revenue at any facility they own or control after a three-year window, forcing divestment of the hospitals they hold as investments. Private equity ownership of hospitals has been tied to cost-cutting and facility closures, so the firms' financial interest here runs against the patients in those communities.

REITs often own hospital land and buildings as a financing arrangement; the bill's broad definition of control could sweep in ownership and management contracts, requiring sales or restructuring. Some REIT arrangements are pure financing, so the effect on patient care is less direct than for private equity operators.

analysis.trajectory: With three Democratic sponsors, no Republican support, and no action from the Senate Finance Committee, this bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a vote this Congress. Bills referred to Finance generally die there unless committee leadership or bipartisan sponsors push them.
